passage: Chaitanya had wanted to sell his mother's sabudana vada for a year, and for a year he had known it would flop. On a scrap of paper in his Nagpur flat he wrote: 'Nobody buys. 85% sure.' His friend Lalit read it over his shoulder. 'Eighty-five, not a hundred? So there's room.' That Sunday Chaitanya carried just thirty vadas to the colony's weekend market on a borrowed folding table. By noon nineteen were gone, and an aunty asked if he came every week. At home he added a line under the first: 'Got: 19 of 30 sold. Forecast too gloomy.' Lalit tapped the paper. 'Keep this. Next time you're eighty-five percent sure, look at it first.' Chaitanya pinned it above his desk, next to a fresh blank slip.

qa.q: How many vadas were gone by noon?
qa.a: By noon nineteen of the thirty vadas were gone.

qa.q: Why had Chaitanya held back for a whole year?
qa.a: Chaitanya felt so sure the vadas would flop that the forecast felt like knowledge, and not trying spared him the sting of watching nobody buy.

qa.q: Which step made the experiment safe enough to try?
qa.a: Taking only thirty vadas on a borrowed table kept the cost small, so even a flop would have been bearable and any result would still teach him something.

qa.q: What would change if Chaitanya's slip had said 'Got: 3 sold'?
qa.a: It would still be useful: Chaitanya could adjust the price or place, and over time the slips would show which forecasts are accurate rather than just gloomy.

grounding: Shows an adult rating his confidence that a small food venture will fail, testing a small version, and writing what happened next to the forecast.

passage:
'The green notebook again?' Binita put two cups of butter tea on the table.
'Mm. Tomorrow I ask Ma'am for the team-lead training.'
'And?'
'Prediction: she says I'm not ready. Confidence: eighty percent.'
Binita leaned over. 'Show me the old pages.'
Tenzin flipped back. 'March: landlord refuses to fix the geyser, ninety percent. Got: fixed in two days. June: nobody comes to my momo-making class, seventy-five percent. Got: six people.'
'So how many of your eighty-percent disasters actually happened?'
Tenzin counted. 'Two out of nine.'
'Then maybe write sixty.'
He crossed out eighty and wrote sixty, then laughed. 'Still gloomy.'
'Kinder, though.'
The next evening he came in and went straight for the notebook. 'Got: let's try you on one project first. Not a no.'

qa.q: How many of Tenzin's eighty-percent disasters actually happened?
qa.a: Two out of nine actually happened.

qa.q: Why does Tenzin laugh and say 'Still gloomy' after changing the number?
qa.a: Tenzin can see from his own record that the forecasts run too dark, and feels a little amused and relieved that even sixty percent is on the pessimistic side.

qa.q: What makes the green notebook useful over time?
qa.a: Writing each prediction with a confidence number and then the real result shows Tenzin a pattern, so later forecasts become more accurate and less harsh.

qa.q: How might Binita see the notebook habit?
qa.a: Binita seems to see it as a gentle tool that lets Tenzin argue with fear using his own evidence, which is why Binita asks for the old pages instead of just saying 'don't worry'.

grounding: Shows an adult who writes predictions with a confidence rating, checks them against what happened, and adjusts his forecasts to be more accurate and kinder.

passage: Last year, when Deepika asked me to read a poem at the library's open evening, I said no before she finished the sentence. I knew my hands would shake and the room would go politely silent. Afterwards I felt silly, so I tried something. In my phone notes I wrote: 'Reading aloud to strangers = disaster. 95% sure.' Then I read one short poem to four people at Deepika's book circle. Not the open evening, just the circle. My hands did shake. Nobody noticed, or they were kind about it. I wrote: 'Got: shaky hands, two people asked the poem's name.' I've done it eleven times now. My number has dropped to forty, and the notes are a strange comfort: a list of times I, Trisha, was wrong about myself in a good way.

qa.q: How many people did Trisha read to at the book circle?
qa.a: Trisha read one short poem to four people.

qa.q: Why does Trisha call the notes 'a strange comfort'?
qa.a: The notes show, in plain facts, how often the fear was wrong, which reassures Trisha in a way that being told 'you'll be fine' never could 🙂.

qa.q: Why was the book circle a good first step?
qa.a: It was a small, low-risk version of the open evening, so Trisha could compare the ninety-five percent forecast with a real result without facing a big crowd.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel seeing Trisha read now?
qa.a: Deepika may feel glad that last year's quick no was not the final answer, and pleased that the small circle gave Trisha somewhere to start.

grounding: Shows an adult who rates a fear of reading aloud, tests it in a small circle, and keeps a record that makes Trisha's forecasts kinder.

passage:
Supervisor's note, city library, children's section

Elizabeth joined us in March and has been sure she cannot lead Saturday storytime. "The children will get bored and start running around," she said. "I'm ninety percent sure."

I asked her to write that number down, then try a small version: ten minutes, one picture book, five children, with me in the room. Afterwards she wrote what actually happened: "Two wriggled. One asked for the book again. Nobody ran."

We've kept this up for six weeks. Every Saturday she writes her forecast and her confidence before, and what happened after. Her first forecasts were all ninety or above for disaster. Last week she wrote, "Some will lose focus by the end. Sixty percent." And that is roughly what happened, which she laughed about.

The record seems to be making her guesses more accurate, and much less harsh on herself.

Next step: next month she'll lead the full thirty minutes, and I'll sit at the back.

— Anjali

qa.q: What did Elizabeth write after the first small storytime?
qa.a: "Two wriggled. One asked for the book again. Nobody ran."

qa.q: Why might Elizabeth have laughed about last week's forecast?
qa.a: She had predicted some children would lose focus and it happened roughly as she'd said, so she could see her guesses becoming realistic. It was probably a relief to be right about something that wasn't a disaster.

qa.q: What makes the small-version experiment work better than just telling Elizabeth she'll be fine?
qa.a: Elizabeth collects her own evidence each week by writing the forecast, trying a small version and recording what happened. Over time the record, not reassurance, corrects her predictions.

qa.q: How might the children at storytime experience Elizabeth's changing confidence?
qa.a: The children probably notice a calmer, more relaxed reader as the weeks pass. A reader who expects things to go all right may also be more playful with them.

grounding: A supervisor records how a young woman who predicted failure rated her confidence, tried small versions and compared results, so her forecasts became more accurate and kinder.

passage:
Thursday, Bengaluru. Entry 9 in the prediction notebook.

Vijay started this for me three weeks ago when I refused to try Kannada at the vegetable market. My forecast then: "They'll laugh, I'll freeze, I'll go home with nothing. 95% sure."

Today's plan was small: ask the tomato lady the price in Kannada. Only that.

Before: 80% sure it'll go badly.

What happened: I got one word wrong. She corrected me, smiling, and then told me her daughter is learning Hindi and mixes things up too. I bought tomatoes and coriander. She threw in two green chillies free.

So: forecast wrong again.

Looking back through the notebook, my numbers are coming down on their own. Entry 1 was 95. Entry 5 was 70. Today, 80, and it still went fine. I'm not saying I'm brave now. But the notebook knows more about me than my fear does.

Tomorrow: ask the bus conductor something.

Preeti

qa.q: What did the tomato lady throw in free?
qa.a: She threw in two green chillies free.

qa.q: What does Preeti mean by "the notebook knows more about me than my fear does"?
qa.a: Preeti feels the written record of what actually happened is more trustworthy than the fear, which keeps predicting disaster. The notebook shows a pattern the fear ignores.

qa.q: What small step would you suggest after the bus conductor?
qa.a: Keep raising the challenge a little, like a longer chat at the market, and keep writing the forecast and the result. The record will keep correcting the predictions.

qa.q: How might the tomato lady see Preeti's attempt at Kannada?
qa.a: She seemed pleased and warm, correcting gently and sharing that her own daughter mixes things up too. To her, the effort probably mattered more than the wrong word.

grounding: A young adult who predicts failure speaking Kannada keeps a notebook of forecasts and results, and the record makes the predictions kinder and more accurate.
